questions.prompt: What does Q#'s `use` statement do?
options: Imports a namespace from another file
Allocates one or more qubits, scoped to the surrounding block
Declares a classical variable as mutable
Submits a job to Azure Quantum
questions.explain: `use q = Qubit();` (or `use qs = Qubit[n];`) is the modern QDK syntax for allocating qubits, scoped to the block they're declared in, replacing the deprecated `using` block style.

questions.prompt: A team is deciding between Q#/Azure Quantum and Qiskit for a new project. Based on this course's framing, which of the following are legitimate reasons to reach for Q# specifically? (Select all that apply.)
options: They need a pre-fault-tolerant hardware resourcing estimate for a proposal
They want a standalone, compiled, type-checked language rather than a Python library
They need to interactively redraw and transpile circuits as Python objects during exploratory research
They are building a large, modular, team-maintained quantum codebase
questions.explain: Resource estimation, the standalone compiled/typed nature of Q#, and large modular codebases are all Q#-favoring reasons covered in this course. Interactive circuit redrawing/transpiling-as-data is specifically a Qiskit strength, not a reason to choose Q#.

questions.prompt: In Q#, an operation that performs no quantum measurement and has no meaningful return value is declared with a return type of ____.
questions.explain: Operations with no meaningful value to return (most gate-applying operations) are declared `: Unit`, Q#'s equivalent of 'no return value'.

questions.prompt: A student writes an operation that allocates a qubit with `use q = Qubit();`, applies `H(q)`, and measures with `M(q)` -- but never explicitly resets the qubit before the end of the block. What is the realistic concern this raises, based on the course's coverage of qubit allocation?
options: There is no concern; measurement always resets the qubit automatically in every case

Depending on the simulator/target, a qubit may need to be returned to |0> or measured before its implicit release at end of scope -- an unmeasured, non-|0> qubit at release time can be a real issue on some targets
The program will fail to compile because `use` requires an explicit `Reset(q)` call before the closing brace in every case
Qubits in Q# never need to be released at all
questions.explain: Lesson 6 covers that qubits allocated via `use` are released automatically at end of scope, and many targets expect them to be measured or reset to |0> first -- this is a real, non-trivial nuance, not an automatic non-issue.

questions.prompt: The Chapter 1 fundamentals lab builds a 2-qubit Bell state (H then CNOT) and reasons about expected measurement correlations. Based on the verified probabilities from this course, which outcomes have nonzero probability? (Select all that apply.)
options: Both qubits measured as Zero (00)
Both qubits measured as One (11)
First Zero, second One (01)
First One, second Zero (10)
questions.explain: The Bell state (|00>+|11>)/sqrt(2) has probability exactly 0.5 on 00 and 0.5 on 11, verified by explicit matrix computation, with exactly 0 probability on 01 and 10.

questions.prompt: What does declaring a Q# operation `is Adj + Ctl` actually provide?
options: Faster simulation performance only
Compiler-generated Adjoint (inverse) and Controlled variants of the operation, derived automatically from its body
Automatic measurement of all qubits used in the operation
Permission to call the operation from inside a `function`
questions.explain: `is Adj + Ctl` tells the compiler to derive both the inverse and the control-gated version of the operation automatically -- a compiler guarantee, not a runtime or library-level feature.

questions.prompt: Which of the following statements about Q#'s operation/function distinction are true, based on this course? (Select all that apply.)
options: A `function` can be called from inside an `operation`, but a quantum-side-effecting `operation` cannot be called from inside a `function`
The compiler enforces this separation; it is not just a naming convention
Qiskit has an equivalent compiler-enforced separation between classical helper code and circuit-building code
A `function` must be pure and deterministic, with no qubits and no randomness
questions.explain: Functions can be called from operations but not vice versa for quantum side effects, and this is compiler-checked. Qiskit has no equivalent enforced boundary -- both classical and circuit-building code are just Python, which is the explicit contrast drawn in Chapter 2 and revisited in Chapter 6.

questions.prompt: The two-qubit intrinsic gate commonly used to entangle qubits, which flips the target qubit only when the control qubit is |1>, is called ____.
questions.explain: CNOT (or equivalently `Controlled X` applied with one control) flips the target qubit's state only when the control qubit is |1>, and is the standard entangling gate used throughout this course (Bell states, GHZ states, teleportation).

questions.prompt: A developer tries to declare an operation `is Adj` where the operation body internally calls `M` (measurement) on a qubit. What happens, and why?
options: It compiles successfully; Adjoint simply skips the measurement when the inverse is called
The compiler rejects the `is Adj` declaration at compile time, because measurement is not unitary and has no well-defined inverse
It compiles, but crashes at runtime the first time Adjoint is called
It compiles and silently returns an incorrect but valid-looking inverse
questions.explain: Measurement collapses state irreversibly and has no valid inverse; the Q# compiler checks this and rejects the is Adj claim at compile time, catching the problem before runtime -- a direct consequence of functors being a compiler-checked guarantee.

questions.prompt: For a composed operation like `EncodeAngle` (which applies `Ry(theta)` then `S`), which of the following correctly describe how the compiler-generated Adjoint behaves? (Select all that apply.)
options: It reverses the order of the original sequence
It applies the adjoint of each individual step
It applies Adjoint S first, then Adjoint Ry(theta)
It applies Ry(theta) then S again unchanged
questions.explain: Correctly inverting a composed sequence of unitary operations requires both reversing the order AND inverting each step -- exactly what the compiler derives automatically, giving 'Adjoint S, then Adjoint Ry(theta)' for this example.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are real prerequisites or components of creating an Azure Quantum workspace, per this course? (Select all that apply.)
options: A resource group inside an Azure subscription
A linked Azure Storage account
At least one provider explicitly added to the workspace
A pre-written Q# program uploaded during workspace creation
questions.explain: A workspace needs a resource group/subscription, a linked storage account for job data, and explicitly added providers -- there is no requirement to upload any program during workspace creation itself.

questions.prompt: A team has just finished writing a new Q# algorithm and wants to know whether it's even plausible to run on hardware that doesn't exist yet, before spending more research time on it. Which Azure Quantum target should they use first?
options: Real hardware (a QPU provider), to get a genuine result immediately
The resource estimator, since it's designed exactly for projecting feasibility on future fault-tolerant hardware without needing that hardware to exist
A local simulator, since it will give them a feasibility projection for fault-tolerant hardware
None of the targets can answer this question
questions.explain: The resource estimator is purpose-built for exactly this question -- projecting physical qubit/runtime needs on future fault-tolerant hardware. A simulator only gives exact results for what it can represent today; it says nothing about future hardware feasibility.

questions.prompt: The Azure Quantum service that projects the physical qubit count and runtime an algorithm would need on future fault-tolerant hardware, without actually executing the program, is called the ____.
questions.explain: The Resource Estimator is the distinctive, first-class Azure Quantum service covered in Chapter 3 and revisited in the Chapter 6 comparison, projecting hardware requirements rather than executing the program for a result.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are genuine operational concerns when submitting jobs to real Azure Quantum hardware providers, according to this course? (Select all that apply.)
options: Jobs can queue in a 'Waiting' state behind other customers' jobs on the same physical device
Real hardware jobs can accrue cost per job or per shot
Resource estimator jobs accrue the same per-shot hardware cost as real QPU jobs
Dry-running on a simulator first avoids paying for and waiting on a job that was going to fail for logic reasons anyway
questions.explain: Queueing and real cost accrual are genuine concerns for real hardware jobs, and dry-running on a simulator first avoids wasting time/money on logic bugs. The resource estimator is explicitly a free, non-executing projection service -- it does not accrue the same per-shot hardware cost as a real QPU job.

questions.prompt: A developer submits a job via `workspace.submit(program, target="ionq.simulator", shots=1000)` and then calls `job.wait_until_completed()`. What is this call actually doing?
options: Cancelling the job immediately
Blocking the script while internally polling the job's status (Waiting/Executing/Succeeded/Failed) until it reaches a terminal state
Resubmitting the job to a different, cheaper target automatically
Converting the simulator job into a real-hardware job
questions.explain: wait_until_completed() performs the same status-polling loop you'd otherwise write by hand with repeated job-show calls, blocking until the job reaches Succeeded or Failed.

questions.prompt: For a 2-qubit search space (N=4) with exactly one marked item and exactly one Grover iteration, this course verified the exact resulting probability of measuring the marked item by direct matrix computation. What was that verified value?
options: Approximately 0.95
Exactly 1.0
Exactly 0.5
Exactly 0.25, unchanged from the uniform starting distribution
questions.explain: Building the 4-dimensional state vector and applying the oracle's sign flip followed by the diffusion reflection gave exactly [0,0,0,1.0] -- probability 1.0 on the marked item, a special case where N=4 with 1 marked item hits the optimal iteration count exactly on the first try.

questions.prompt: Based on the verified QFT computation for a 2-qubit input state |01>, which of the following are true? (Select all that apply.)
options: All four output basis states have the same probability of being measured (0.25 each)
The output phases step by 90 degrees between consecutive basis state indices
Measuring the QFT output directly reveals the original input index j with certainty
The QFT is a change of basis, not a computation that produces a single definite 'answer'
questions.explain: The verified computation showed magnitude 0.5 (probability 0.25) on every output with phases stepping by 90 degrees. Since every outcome is equally likely, measuring the output alone reveals nothing about which input it came from -- which is exactly why QFT is embedded inside phase estimation rather than measured on its own.

questions.prompt: In the verified teleportation example (teleporting |+>), each of the 4 possible Bell-measurement outcomes (m1, m2) occurs with probability exactly ____.
questions.explain: Direct matrix computation of the full 3-qubit state, after applying CNOT and H to the sender's two qubits, confirmed each of the 4 outcomes occurs with probability exactly 0.25 -- not approximately, exactly.

questions.prompt: The Chapter 4 algorithms lab extended Grover's to mark 2 items out of 4 (N=4) and ran exactly one iteration. What was the verified result, and what does it demonstrate?
options: Probability 1.0 on each marked item, showing 2 marked items amplify twice as fast
Probability exactly 0.25 on all four items -- identical to the starting uniform distribution, demonstrating that the correct iteration count depends on the actual number of marked items, not just N
Probability 0 on all items, showing Grover's algorithm fails with more than one marked item
The result could not be computed without running real hardware
questions.explain: With 2 of 4 items marked, the diffusion step's driving inner product canceled exactly to zero, leaving probabilities at [0.25,0.25,0.25,0.25] -- identical to the starting distribution, demonstrating that guessing the wrong iteration count for the actual M can eliminate any benefit entirely.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly explain why quantum teleportation does not allow faster-than-light communication? (Select all that apply.)
options: The receiver's qubit alone, without the classical bits m1/m2, looks identical no matter what the sender measured
The actual information needed to apply the correct correction travels only via the 2 classical bits, which cannot exceed light speed
Entanglement alone instantaneously transmits the classical bits needed for correction
Each of the 4 possible outcomes is equally likely, so no outcome by itself reveals information to the receiver without the classical bits
questions.explain: The receiver's qubit is indistinguishable across outcomes without the classical bits, those bits travel at or below light speed, and no single equally-likely outcome reveals information on its own. Entanglement enables the correlation but does not itself transmit the classical bits -- that's exactly the misconception the lesson corrects.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly describe real pieces of the Q#/Python interoperability workflow covered in this course? (Select all that apply.)
options: `%%qsharp` cell magic compiles Q# source directly inside a Jupyter notebook cell
`qsharp.run(op, shots=N)` performs native repeated sampling in one call, rather than looping Python calls one at a time
`qsharp.estimate(...)` submits the program directly to real Azure Quantum hardware
`azure-quantum`'s `Workspace.submit()` connects a compiled program to a real cloud target
questions.explain: %%qsharp, qsharp.run, and Workspace.submit() are all real, correctly-described pieces of the workflow. qsharp.estimate() produces a resource-estimate report locally -- it does not submit to real hardware, which is a distinct step handled by azure-quantum's Workspace.

questions.prompt: A developer needs to collect 5,000 measurement samples from a Q# operation as part of a Python experiment script. Which approach does this course recommend as more idiomatic and efficient?
options: A Python for-loop calling `qsharp.eval(...)` 5,000 times
`qsharp.run("Op()", shots=5000)`, which performs the sampling natively in one call
Manually rewriting the operation in Python using numpy
Submitting 5,000 separate jobs to Azure Quantum hardware
questions.explain: qsharp.run(shots=N) does the repeated sampling natively, avoiding the overhead of 5,000 separate round-trips into the Q# runtime from a Python loop.

questions.prompt: In the Interoperability Lab's verified GHZ-state computation (H then two CNOTs on 3 qubits), the probability of measuring the outcome '000' is exactly ____.
questions.explain: Direct matrix computation of the 3-qubit GHZ state showed nonzero amplitude only on |000> and |111>, each with probability exactly 0.5, and exactly 0 probability on all six other possible 3-bit outcomes.

questions.prompt: Which of the following are reasons given in this course for keeping Q# source (under `src/` with `qsharp.json`) in a separate folder from Python orchestration code (under `experiments/`)? (Select all that apply.)
options: The Q# project becomes independently compilable, testable, and resource-estimable without any Python involved
It makes it obvious, by folder structure alone, which code is quantum-algorithmic versus classical orchestration
Python cannot technically call into Q# code unless the files are in separate folders
It mirrors, at the project level, the same operation/function separation the Q# compiler enforces at the language level
questions.explain: The separation gives independent testability/estimation and clarity by folder structure, and mirrors the language-level operation/function boundary. It is a matter of good organization, not a technical requirement -- Python can call into Q# regardless of folder layout as long as qsharp.init() points at the right project root.

questions.prompt: A developer edits a `.qs` file in an active `qsharp.init()` session, but a Python variable that already held a reference to the old compiled operation still behaves as before the edit. What does this course identify as the likely cause?
options: Q# does not support editing files during an active session at all
The stale Python-side reference still points to the previously compiled version; re-fetching or re-calling the operation is the first thing to check
The edit was automatically reverted by the compiler
Jupyter notebooks cannot detect file changes under any circumstances
questions.explain: Recompilation happens automatically on edit within an active session, but a Python-side variable already holding a reference to the old compiled callable may not reflect the change until re-fetched -- the specific gotcha called out in Lesson 21.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly capture the design-philosophy comparison this course draws between Qiskit and Q#? (Select all that apply.)
options: A Qiskit QuantumCircuit is mutable, inspectable Python data you can draw, transpile, and compose at runtime
A Q# operation is a compiled unit of computation, with no equivalent intermediate inspectable object between code and execution
Q#'s compiler-checked functors and operation/function split are a type-system guarantee that Qiskit's library-level `.inverse()`/`.control()` do not provide
Qiskit cannot express any of the algorithms (Grover's, QFT, teleportation) that Q# can express
questions.explain: The first three are the lesson's actual comparative claims. The fourth is explicitly false -- the course is clear that both tools can express the same algorithms; the difference is the programming model and its tradeoffs, not raw capability.

questions.prompt: A hardware research team needs a standardized, free, pre-fault-tolerant hardware-resourcing estimate for a roadmap decision years before the hardware exists. Based on this course's decision framework, which tool fits this specific task, and why?
options: Qiskit, because its transpiler produces circuit depth and gate counts
Q#/Azure Quantum Resource Estimator, because it is the standardized, integrated, free service purpose-built for exactly this fault-tolerant-planning question
Either tool works identically well for this specific task
Neither tool can answer this kind of question
questions.explain: This is the clearest-cut scenario in the course's decision framework: the Resource Estimator is specifically designed for this exact question, with no equivalent single integrated tool in Qiskit's core toolchain.

questions.prompt: In the capstone's ported Bell-state circuit (H then CNOT, implemented identically in both Qiskit and Q#), the verified probability of measuring the outcome '01' is exactly ____.
questions.explain: Direct matrix computation showed the Bell state has amplitude exactly 1/sqrt(2) on |00> and |11> only, with exactly zero amplitude -- and therefore zero probability -- on |01> and |10>, confirmed identically for both the Qiskit and Q# implementations of the same circuit.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly describe the comparison this course draws between Qiskit's and Azure Quantum's resource-estimation approaches? (Select all that apply.)
options: Qiskit's transpiler/depth-analysis tools target near-term, real-hardware feasibility questions (today's connectivity, gate fidelity)
Azure Quantum's Resource Estimator targets future fault-tolerant hardware cost projection, independent of today's connectivity constraints
The two approaches are competing solutions to the identical question, and one is simply better than the other
For the SAME algorithm, elementary gate/step counts don't change based on which language implements it -- the real distinction is about standardized future-hardware projection, not gate counting
questions.explain: The first, second, and fourth statements are the lesson's actual, careful claims. The third is explicitly rejected by the lesson -- these are different questions for different hardware eras, not rival answers to the same question.

questions.prompt: A solo developer is interactively exploring a novel algorithm variant, wants to redraw and reshape the circuit on the fly, and wants tight integration with numpy/matplotlib for live plotting. Using this course's decision framework, which tool fits best, and which specific mechanism justifies it?
options: Q#, because its compiler-enforced operation/function split prevents bugs during interactive exploration

Qiskit, because its circuit-as-data model lets the circuit be inspected, redrawn, and reshaped at runtime, and the whole workflow stays in the same Python process as numpy/matplotlib with no bridge to cross
Q#, because the Azure Quantum Resource Estimator is required for any interactive exploration
Neither tool supports interactive exploration with plotting libraries
questions.explain: This scenario matches Qiskit's specific strength from the decision framework: circuit-as-data makes runtime inspection/reshaping natural, and there's no Q#-to-Python bridge to cross since Qiskit never leaves Python in the first place.
